readAloud.text: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing the way scientific research is conducted. Machine learning systems can analyse enormous datasets in hours, identifying patterns that would take human researchers years to discover. In medicine, these systems already help doctors detect diseases earlier and design new drugs. Nevertheless, experts caution that human judgement remains essential for interpreting results and making ethical decisions.

Every year, an estimated eleven million tonnes of plastic waste enter the world's oceans. Rivers carry discarded packaging, bottles, and fishing gear from the land to the sea, where sunlight and waves slowly break them into microscopic fragments. These microplastics have now been found everywhere from the deepest ocean trenches to Arctic sea ice, and their long-term effects on marine life remain poorly understood.

Electric aviation promises to transform regional air travel over the coming decades. Battery-powered aircraft produce no emissions during flight and are far quieter than conventional planes, which could allow airports to operate longer hours without disturbing nearby residents. The main obstacle is battery weight: current technology limits electric planes to short routes with few passengers, but engineers expect steady improvements.

The fashion industry produces more clothing than ever before, yet the average garment is worn fewer times. Fast fashion brands release new styles weekly, encouraging consumers to treat clothing as disposable. This model consumes vast quantities of water, generates enormous textile waste, and accounts for a significant share of global carbon emissions. Campaigners argue that both companies and consumers must rethink their relationship with clothing.

Populations are ageing rapidly across much of the developed world. As birth rates fall and life expectancy rises, the proportion of citizens over sixty-five continues to grow. This demographic shift places considerable pressure on pension systems, healthcare services, and the labour market. Governments are responding with measures such as raising retirement ages, encouraging older workers to remain employed, and cautiously expanding immigration.

Museums have undergone a quiet revolution in recent decades. Once regarded as dusty storehouses of artefacts, they now compete to offer interactive exhibitions, digital archives, and educational programmes for schools. Many institutions have also begun to confront uncomfortable questions about how their collections were acquired, and several prominent museums have returned objects to the communities from which they were originally taken.

Fresh water covers only a tiny fraction of the planet's surface, yet demand for it continues to rise. Agriculture consumes roughly seventy percent of global freshwater supplies, and inefficient irrigation wastes much of it. Meanwhile, climate change is altering rainfall patterns, leaving some regions with too little water and others with destructive floods. Experts warn that water scarcity could become one of the defining crises of this century.

retellLecture.title: The business of space tourism
retellLecture.sample: The lecture described how space tourism developed from one expensive private trip in 2001 into a growing commercial industry. The speaker explained that companies now offer short suborbital flights and predicted that ticket prices will fall as rockets become reusable, just as airfares once did. However, the lecture also noted major obstacles, including safety concerns, the environmental impact of launches, and the huge cost of building vehicles that can reach orbit.
retellLecture.text: Space tourism has shifted from science fiction to a genuine industry in a remarkably short time. The first private passenger paid twenty million dollars for a trip to the International Space Station in 2001. Two decades later, several companies began offering suborbital flights that give passengers a few minutes of weightlessness and a view of the Earth's curve, for a fraction of that price. Industry analysts predict that ticket costs will continue to fall as rockets become reusable, much as airfares dropped in the early days of aviation. Nevertheless, significant obstacles remain, including safety concerns, the environmental impact of launches, and the enormous cost of building larger vehicles capable of reaching orbit.

retellLecture.title: Gene editing and its promise
retellLecture.sample: The lecturer introduced CRISPR, a cheap and precise gene-editing tool originally borrowed from bacteria. The speaker listed its main applications, including curing inherited diseases, creating drought-resistant crops, and fighting malaria, and mentioned the first approved CRISPR therapy in 2023. Finally, the lecture warned that editing embryos raises serious ethical questions because the changes pass to future generations, so most scientists support strict limits on the technology.
retellLecture.text: Few technologies have excited biologists as much as CRISPR, a gene-editing tool adapted from a defence system found in bacteria. CRISPR allows researchers to cut DNA at precise locations and rewrite the genetic code, at a fraction of the cost of earlier methods. Its potential applications are enormous: correcting inherited diseases, engineering crops that survive drought, and eliminating the mosquitoes that spread malaria. The first CRISPR-based therapy, for sickle-cell disease, was approved in 2023 and has already transformed patients' lives. Yet the technology raises difficult questions. Editing embryos would create changes that pass to future generations, and a scientist who did exactly that in 2018 was imprisoned. Most researchers therefore support strict limits on how far gene editing should go.

respondToSituation.prompt: You share a flat with another student. Your flatmate keeps leaving the heating and lights on all day, and your electricity bill has doubled. Talk to your flatmate about the problem. What would you say?
respondToSituation.audio: You share a flat with another student. Your flatmate keeps leaving the heating and lights on all day, and your electricity bill has doubled. Talk to your flatmate about the problem. What would you say?
respondToSituation.sample: Hey, can I talk to you about the electricity bill? It arrived this morning and it's nearly double what we normally pay. I think it's because the heating's been left on all day when nobody's home, and the kitchen lights stay on overnight. I know you're not doing it on purpose, but I honestly can't afford this on my student budget. Could we agree to turn the heating off whenever we go out, and maybe check the lights before bed? If it helps, I can put little reminder notes by the switches. I really don't want this to become a problem between us — I just need us both to be a bit more careful. Thanks for understanding.

respondToSituation.prompt: You are part of a group of four students preparing a presentation. One member has missed every meeting and has not replied to messages. The presentation is next week. Talk to that group member. What would you say?
respondToSituation.audio: You are part of a group of four students preparing a presentation. One member has missed every meeting and has not replied to messages. The presentation is next week. Talk to that group member. What would you say?
respondToSituation.sample: Hi, thanks for meeting me. Look, I'm a bit worried about the group presentation. You've missed the last three meetings and we haven't heard back from you, so we weren't sure if you're still doing the project. If something's going on, that's completely fine — just tell us and we can work around it. But the presentation is next Thursday, and your section on the survey results still isn't started. We really need you to send us your slides by Sunday so we can rehearse together on Monday. Can you commit to that? And if you can't, please be honest with me now, and we'll divide your part between the rest of us. I just don't want anyone to fail because of a communication problem.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: Should lectures be recorded and attendance made optional?
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The group discussed whether recorded lectures should make attendance optional. Speaker A supported recordings because they help students with jobs, illness, or weaker English, and believed attendance should not be compulsory. Speaker B warned that recordings lead to empty lecture halls and weaker discussion, proposing participation incentives such as in-class quizzes. Speaker C cited research suggesting students use recordings mainly for revision and suggested a compromise: record everything, keep attendance optional, but build interactive elements into lectures. The speakers broadly converged on this middle position.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: I think recording lectures is obviously a good thing. Students who are ill, or who have jobs or caring responsibilities, shouldn't be penalised. If the lecture is online, attendance shouldn't be compulsory.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I disagree. The moment recordings go online, half the class stops turning up. Discussion dies, and lecturers end up talking to an empty room. Learning is a social activity, not just content delivery.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Both of you have a point, but the research I've seen says recordings are mainly used for revision before exams, not as a substitute for attending. Students still come when the lecture is engaging.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Exactly. And for students whose first language isn't English, being able to replay difficult sections is a huge help.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's true, but I'd still keep some kind of participation requirement, maybe in-class quizzes, so there's an incentive to attend.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: So maybe the compromise is: record everything, keep attendance optional, but build interactive elements into lectures so people actually want to be there.

summarizeGroupDiscussion.topic: The student union is considering banning smartphones during seminars. Discuss.
summarizeGroupDiscussion.sample: The students debated banning smartphones in seminars. Speaker A supported the ban, arguing that phones are disrespectful to tutors and damage group discussion. Speaker B opposed a total ban as heavy-handed, pointing out that phones are useful for looking up terms and taking notes. Speaker C proposed distinguishing seminars from lectures and suggested a shared 'phones face down' norm rather than a formal ban. In the end, all three agreed that seminars should be phone-free, with exceptions for accessibility needs, while lectures should remain unrestricted.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Honestly, I'd support a ban. In my seminars, half the people are scrolling under the table. It's disrespectful to the tutor and it ruins the discussion for everyone else.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I get that, but a total ban feels heavy-handed. I use my phone to look up terms I don't understand and to take notes. Treating adults like schoolchildren isn't the answer.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Could we distinguish between lectures and seminars? In a seminar you need to be fully present, so maybe phones away makes sense there. In lectures, let people manage their own attention.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: That's reasonable. It's really the small-group discussions that suffer.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: I'd accept that, as long as there are exceptions for accessibility needs and note-taking apps.

turns.speaker: C
turns.text: Agreed. We could suggest a 'phones face down' policy for seminars rather than a formal ban, so it feels like a shared norm instead of a punishment.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Space tourism moved from fantasy to reality in the early 2020s, when private companies began flying paying passengers to the edge of space. Tickets cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, putting the experience far beyond the reach of ordinary people. Supporters argue that the industry drives technological innovation and that prices will fall as the technology matures, just as air travel became affordable over the course of the twentieth century. Critics counter that rocket launches release carbon emissions and black carbon high in the atmosphere, where their warming effect is strongest, and they question the value of spending billions on brief joyrides while pressing problems remain unsolved on Earth. Whether space tourism becomes a mature mass-market industry or remains an expensive novelty will depend on how quickly these economic and environmental challenges can be overcome.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: Space tourism has become a commercial reality that supporters believe will drive innovation and eventually become affordable like air travel, but critics object that its high-altitude emissions worsen climate change and that the money would be better spent on Earth's problems, so its future depends on overcoming economic and environmental obstacles.

summarizeWrittenText.passage: Roughly one third of all food produced for human consumption is never eaten, an astonishing failure in a world where hundreds of millions of people still go hungry. The causes of this waste differ sharply between rich and poor countries. In developing nations, food is lost mainly after harvest, because of inadequate storage, poor roads, and a lack of refrigeration between farm and market. In wealthy nations, by contrast, most waste occurs in supermarkets and homes, where consumers buy more than they need and confusion over date labels leads people to discard food that is perfectly safe. The environmental consequences are severe: food rotting in landfills releases methane, and food waste alone accounts for around eight percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. Researchers therefore argue that reducing waste is among the cheapest and fastest ways to cut emissions and improve food security at the same time.
summarizeWrittenText.sample: A third of all food is wasted for different reasons in rich and poor countries — poor storage and transport in developing nations versus overbuying and date-label confusion in wealthy ones — and because this waste causes hunger and significant methane emissions, reducing it is considered one of the cheapest ways to cut emissions and improve food security.

essay.prompt: Some people believe that artificial intelligence and automation will create more jobs than they destroy, while others argue they pose a serious threat to employment. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write 200–300 words.
essay.sample: Possible structure: (1) Introduction — paraphrase the debate, state your position. (2) Optimist view: past technologies created new industries, AI removes boring tasks and creates roles in data, maintenance and design, higher productivity raises living standards. (3) Pessimist view: automation now threatens white-collar as well as manual jobs, new roles require skills displaced workers lack, transition may be painful and unequal. (4) Conclusion — your view, e.g. jobs will change more than disappear, but governments must invest in retraining. Useful phrases: 'It is often argued that…', 'A compelling argument is…', 'On the other hand…', 'History suggests that…', 'In conclusion, I believe…'

summarizeSpokenText.title: The economics of food waste
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The speaker explained that around a billion tonnes of food is wasted every year while many people go hungry. The causes differ: poor countries lose food after harvest because of bad storage and transport, while wealthy countries waste food in shops and homes due to overbuying and confusing date labels. The lecture concluded that food waste causes significant methane emissions, so reducing it is a cheap and fast way to cut emissions and improve food security.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Every year, humanity throws away roughly one billion tonnes of food, while hundreds of millions of people go hungry. The causes differ between rich and poor countries. In developing nations, food is mainly lost after harvest, because of poor storage, bad roads, and a lack of refrigeration. In wealthy nations, most waste happens in shops and homes, where consumers buy more than they need, and confusion over date labels leads people to discard food that is still safe. The environmental cost is staggering: rotting food in landfills produces methane, and food waste alone accounts for around eight percent of global emissions. Researchers argue that reducing waste is one of the cheapest and quickest ways to cut emissions and improve food security.

summarizeSpokenText.title: How AI is changing medical diagnosis
summarizeSpokenText.sample: The lecture described how artificial intelligence is transforming medical diagnosis, especially in image-based fields, where algorithms can detect cancers, eye diseases, and fractures as accurately as specialists. However, the speaker warned that algorithms trained on unrepresentative data perform worse for certain patient groups. The conclusion was that AI will act as a second reader supporting doctors rather than replacing them.
summarizeSpokenText.audio: Artificial intelligence is beginning to transform medical diagnosis, particularly in fields that depend on interpreting images. Algorithms trained on millions of scans can now detect certain cancers, eye diseases, and fractures with an accuracy that matches, and sometimes exceeds, that of experienced specialists. In one trial, an algorithm reviewing mammograms reduced both missed cancers and false alarms. However, researchers stress important limitations. Algorithms learn from historical data, and if that data underrepresents certain groups, the system's accuracy falls for those patients. Most experts therefore believe AI will not replace doctors. Instead, it will act as a second reader, flagging suspicious cases and freeing specialists to focus on complex diagnoses and patient care.

highlightCorrectSummary.audio: Parents often blame social media for teenagers' unhappiness, but recent research paints a more complicated picture. Large studies find only a small statistical link between screen time and depression. What seems to matter far more is how the platforms are used. Teenagers who passively scroll through other people's photos report lower mood, while those who use social media to message close friends often feel more connected. Sleep also plays a crucial role: heavy late-night use disrupts sleep, and it is this lost sleep, rather than screen time itself, that best predicts poor mental health. Researchers therefore advise focusing on habits, not blanket bans.
options: Social media is the main cause of teenage depression, and banning it completely would solve the problem.
The effect of social media depends on how teenagers use it, and lost sleep appears to be a key mechanism behind mental health problems.
Passively scrolling through photos improves teenagers' mood because it provides social connection.
Screen time has no connection whatsoever to teenagers' mental health or sleep.
